section_title: Why does Paul ask to speak to the crowd after being rescued?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 37 As they were about to take Paul into the barracks, he asked the commander, “May I say something to you?” “Do you speak Greek?” he replied. 38 “Aren’t you the Egyptian who incited a rebellion some time ago and led four thousand members of the Assassins into the wilderness?” 39 But Paul answered, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city. Now I beg you to allow me to speak to the people.” 40 Having received permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the crowd. A great hush came over the crowd, and he addressed them in Hebrew:

context_lines: As Paul is about to enter the barracks, he asks the commander in Greek for permission to speak. The commander’s response reveals another mistaken identification: he wonders whether Paul is the Egyptian connected with an earlier rebellion and four thousand members of the Assassins.

Paul answers by identifying himself as a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of a notable city, and asks to address the people. The commander allows it. Paul stands on the steps, signals for quiet and begins speaking in Hebrew.

The scene ends at the opening of the speech continued in Acts 22. Paul has corrected the officer’s assumption and gained a hearing from the crowd. Luke does not say that the officer now believes Paul’s message or that everyone in the crowd has been persuaded.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly see courage and respectful use of an available opportunity here. Paul clarifies who he is and requests permission to speak, rather than accepting either the crowd’s accusation or the commander’s mistaken identity as the last word.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 9:15–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/9.htm) describes Paul’s calling to bear Jesus’ name before Gentiles, rulers and the people of Israel, alongside suffering for that name. Here he stands between a Roman officer and a Jewish crowd, under arrest yet still seeking a hearing. The speech that follows will make his testimony part of the very situation intended to silence him.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
